title: Finlayson Caribou and the KZK Mine Project
text:
1 Introduction
The workbook contains a summary of information sources on the Finlayson Caribou Herd, especially in the context of the Kudz Ze Kayah mine project. In this section, we review the findings of the 2020 report. The other sections provide technical summaries of population estimates, seasonal ranges, and habitat suitability in and around the project area.

title: Finlayson Caribou and the KZK Mine Project
section: 1.1 KZK Screen Report: Finlayson caribou herd
text:
1.1 KZK Screen Report: Finlayson caribou herd
The section regarding the Finlayson caribou herd (FCH) in the Screening Report identifies the Kudz Ze Kayah Project as a source of significant adverse effects to the herd, primarily through habitat displacement and interference with seasonal movements.

1.1.1 Summary of the FCH Assessment

Cultural and Ecological Importance: Caribou are a “cultural keystone species” for the Kaska Dena, as reflected in the project’s name, Kudz Ze Kayah, meaning “land of the caribou”. They are also an umbrella species, meaning protections for them benefit the broader ecosystem.
Current Status: The FCH is a sub-type of woodland caribou designated as a “population of special concern”. The herd is in a persistent decline, dropping approximately 12% between 2007 and 2017 to an estimated 2,700 animals.
Project Impacts:

Habitat Loss: The project is uniquely situated at the intersection of late winter, calving, post-calving, rut, and movement habitats. It will remove approximately 5% of high-quality rutting habitat and 4% of post-calving habitat.
Movement Barriers: The project area is a “caribou crossing” and a portal to critical calving areas; disruptions here affect a significant proportion of the population.
Increased Predation: Clearing the access road in winter facilitates easier movement for wolves, likely increasing predation on caribou.

Recommended Mitigations: The report recommends establishing an oversight body with First Nations representation to manage caribou-specific mitigations adaptively. It also requires the Government of Yukon to develop a comprehensive long-term range management plan for the herd.



1.1.2 Critique of the FCH Section
The report offers a rigorous assessment but highlights several critical information gaps and methodological tensions:

Reliance on Poor Data: The Executive Committee (EC) explicitly notes that available information regarding the FCH is “poor” compared to other Yukon herds. There have been no collaring efforts since the 1980s, and there is a significant lack of data regarding adult mortality.
Unmodeled Impacts: While some habitats were quantified, the EC notes that effects on calving habitat and movement corridors were not modeled, which they describe as a “significant knowledge gap”. This suggests the actual consequences to the population might be higher than the report’s statistics indicate.
Conservative “Zone of Influence”: The Proponent applied a 3 km zone of influence for their models, which the EC notes is on the “lower end” of estimates seen in scientific literature; other studies have shown caribou avoiding mines by up to 23 km.
Conflict Over Significance: There is a clear divergence between the Proponent and the EC. The Proponent argued that because the “human footprint” in the range is only 12%, the project’s magnitude of effect should be considered “low”. The EC countered that caribou may be “naive” to the risks of new industrial footprints, and the herd’s continued decline warrants high caution regardless of the total percentage of disturbed land.
Uncertainty of Reversibility: While the Proponent suggests effects are reversible through reclamation, the EC points out that the effectiveness of many mitigations during operations is largely unknown, and the loss of the open pit and waste storage facilities is permanent and irreversible.

Ultimately, the report concludes that if the project proceeds, the FCH population will likely be lower than it would have been otherwise, placing the herd’s long-term sustainability at risk.

title: 2  YESAB Report 2020
text:
2.1 Strategic Context and Assessment Framework for the FCH
Technical Review and Evolutionary Analysis: Finlayson Caribou Herd (FCH) Assessment for the Kudz Ze Kayah Project
The Finlayson Caribou Herd (FCH) is not merely a biological population; it is a Valued Environmental and Socio-economic Component (VESEC) that serves as the nexus for ecological integrity and the Kaska Way of Life. The 2020 Yukon Environmental and Socio-economic Assessment Board (YESAB) screening represents a landmark in the territory’s regulatory history, as the Executive Committee was forced to reconcile a 38-year industrial lifecycle with the long-term viability of a sensitive woodland caribou population. Under the Yukon Environmental and Socio-economic Assessment Act (YESAA) and the Species at Risk Act (SARA), the assessment framework transitioned from standard project-level mitigation to a rigorous evaluation of the herd’s role in cultural and ecological stability.
By utilizing the Valued Component methodology, the Executive Committee elevated the FCH from a set of isolated biological metrics to a cornerstone of jurisdictional policy. This approach acknowledges that for the Liard First Nation (LFN) and Ross River Dena Council (RRDC), caribou conservation is inseparable from Traditional Land Use and the exercise of Aboriginal rights. The assessment was framed not just by the project footprint, but by the legal necessity to protect the “special relationship between Yukon Indian persons and the wilderness environment.” The 2020 determination was ultimately driven by baseline findings that revealed a herd characterized by significant vulnerability, necessitating a shift toward landscape-level oversight.

title: 2  YESAB Report 2020
section: 2.2 Summary and Evaluation of Section 6.1 Findings (2020)
text:
2.2 Summary and Evaluation of Section 6.1 Findings (2020)
The 2020 baseline findings established that the FCH was in a precarious state long before the proposed commencement of the Kudz Ze Kayah (KZK) Project. A technical understanding of these population trends and spatial requirements was critical to justifying the “Significant Adverse Effect” determination.
Population Metrics and Recruitment Trends
A primary indicator of the herd’s health is the ratio of calves per 100 cows during fall rut surveys, which serves as a proxy for recruitment. Analysis of the data in Figure 17 reveals a critical historical trend: recruitment was significantly higher during the wolf control period (1983-1991). Following the cessation of active predator management, recruitment showed high variability and a general downward pressure. This data highlights the precarious nature of the FCH; the herd lacks the surplus resiliency to absorb additional stressors, making any industrial impact on adult survival or calf recruitment a threat to the population’s self-sustaining status.
Habitat Mapping and the Zone of Influence (ZOI)
Spatial modeling identified that the project directly intersects with high-quality habitat essential for the caribou life cycle:

Seasonal Distribution: The project footprint sits on high-quality suitable habitat used during the Rut and Post-calving periods (Figures 14 and 15), which are the most sensitive phases for population replacement.
Game Management Subzones (GMS): The mine is situated within GMS 10-07, an area that serves as a vital corridor for winter and post-rutting activity.
The 3 km Buffer: Modeling identifies a Zone of Influence (ZOI) extending 3 km from the project boundary (Figure 20). Within this ZOI, sensory disturbances-noise, light, and traffic-are predicted to alter caribou behavior, leading to effective habitat loss and increased energetic costs of displacement.

Significance Determination: The 38-Year Risk
The Executive Committee determined that the project would result in Significant Adverse Effects despite the Proponent’s initial mitigation designs. From a policy perspective, the permanence of the risk is the deciding factor. With a project lifespan of 38 years (construction through post-closure), the duration of displacement exceeds the reproductive lifespan of several generations of caribou. This long-term exclusion from high-quality habitat in GMS 10-07 constitutes a significant threat that standard site-level mitigations cannot resolve. Because the project footprint sits directly on critical Rut and Post-calving habitat, the Committee determined that only the power to seasonally suspend operations could potentially reduce these risks to an acceptable level.

title: 2  YESAB Report 2020
section: 2.3 Critical Analysis of Mandated Mitigations and Oversight
text:
2.3 Critical Analysis of Mandated Mitigations and Oversight
The 2020 Recommendation fundamentally altered the regulatory landscape by moving from “siloed project mitigation” to landscape-level management. This shift moved the primary burden of caribou protection from a Proponent-led model to a government-led co-management framework.
The Oversight Body (Mitigation #10)
The creation of an Oversight Body is a sophisticated regulatory tool designed to manage the energetic costs of displacement in real-time. This body, comprised of the Proponent, Government of Yukon, LFN, and RRDC, possesses the authority to override operational schedules based on caribou presence.

Power to Suspend: The body can mandate the temporary suspension of blasting, crushing, and truck transportation based on seasonal sensitivity.
Sensory Disturbance: Prioritization of methods to reduce noise and light within the ZOI.
Aviation Control: Authority to modify flight paths or enforce a suspension of helicopter use.
Adaptive Triggers: Identification of biological “triggers” that necessitate immediate corrective action and the identification of mitigations based on “New Knowledge” (Mitigation 10.a.v).

FCH Range Management Plan (Mitigation #11)
A significant policy shift occurs in Mitigation #11, which mandates the Government of Yukon to develop a comprehensive plan. This forces a cumulative-effects management style onto the territorial government, ensuring the KZK project is managed within the context of the entire herd range.







Component
Policy Requirement and Scope


a. Management Principles
Must be informed by Traditional Knowledge and the Kaska relationship with caribou.


b. Current Conditions
Identify the health, trend, and condition of the population and habitat using best available info.


c. Limiting Factors
Identify factors including habitat, predation, climate change, and human activities (harvest/land-use).


d. Future Conditions
Scenarios for future impacts from development, wildfire, and climate.


e. Objectives & Thresholds
Specific population/habitat objectives and thresholds of change that cannot be exceeded.


f. Management Tools
Identify voluntary and non-voluntary tools, linked to regulatory and land-use planning.


g. Implementation
Detailed plan for collaborative and timely execution of management actions.


h. Monitoring
Identify ongoing needs, uncertainties, and time-bound learning plans to address data gaps.


i. Adaptive Management
Mechanism for incorporating monitoring results and “new knowledge” into plan revisions.


j. Communication
Establishing methods for sharing results and guidance with communities and decision-makers.



Analytical Insight: By tethering the project’s success to this Range Management Plan, the Yukon Government has effectively ended the era of “site-only” mining assessments. Long-term accountability for the FCH now rests on a collaborative, landscape-wide effort where the Proponent’s social license is contingent upon the broader health of the herd.

title: 2  YESAB Report 2020
section: 2.4 Post-2020 Literature Review: The Evolving Landscape of FCH Conservation
text:
2.4 Post-2020 Literature Review: The Evolving Landscape of FCH Conservation
As per Mitigation 10.a.v, the “New Knowledge” trigger is the primary mechanism for the project to adapt to shifting environmental realities. Since the 2020 screening, the intersection of climate change and industrial disturbance has become even more acute.
Climate-Induced Habitat Shifts and Trigger Application
The 2020 projections-specifically the 2 degree Celsius temperature rise and the trend of snowfall arriving later (Section 5.2)-are no longer distant threats but active management concerns.

Energetic Costs: Warmer, more variable winters lead to increased icing events and deeper, heavier snow. This restricts access to ground lichen and increases the energetic costs of displacement for caribou forced to move away from the project ZOI.
Trigger Mechanism: The “New Knowledge” trigger must now account for the fact that the FCH may be forced to utilize the project area more intensely if surrounding ranges are lost to wildfire or if traditional wintering grounds become energetically too costly to access due to snow conditions.

Indigenous-Led Conservation and Modern Standards
Since 2020, the “Kaska Way of Life” has evolved into a more formal framework for Indigenous-led conservation. Collaborative co-management models have moved beyond simple consultation to active, on-the-ground stewardship. Modern caribou conservation standards now emphasize that sensory disturbance modeling must be coupled with Indigenous observations of herd behavior.
Conclusion: The Necessity of Adaptive Management
The 2020 “Significance Determination” remains robust precisely because it anticipated these shifts. The mitigations provided a “learning loop” via the Oversight Body and the Range Management Plan. However, as climate change accelerates the degradation of caribou habitat, the thresholds of change defined in Mitigation #11 become even more critical. In the current landscape, adaptive management is not an optional administrative process; it is a vital survival mechanism for the Finlayson Caribou Herd and a non-negotiable requirement for the project’s ongoing regulatory compliance.

title: 3  Kudz Ze Kayah
text:
3.1 Predicted residual effects on the FCH
The Kudz Ze Kayah (KZK) project (BMC Minerals Ltd.) is a proposed polymetallic mine located within the Finlayson caribou herd’s spring, summer, and fall range in the Pelly Mountains — the core rut and post-calving habitat. EDI Environmental Dynamics Inc. was retained by YESAB in 2019 to provide an independent review of BMC’s environmental assessment predictions for caribou, moose, and furbearers. The summary below reflects EDI’s findings (Johannesen & Setterington 2019), which largely validated BMC’s conclusions while adding context on cumulative effects and limiting factors.
EDI assessed Project effects using the FCH home range as the Regional Study Area (RSA), applying the same criteria as BMC’s environmental assessment.
Direction: Adverse across all pathways assessed.
Magnitude: Low — the Project footprint affects a small fraction of available FCH habitat within the RSA:

Geographic extent: Local to regional — effects on movement corridors or habitat avoidance could extend beyond the immediate footprint into the broader RSA.
Duration: Long-term — some effects extend into the post-closure phase.
Reversibility: Reversible in the short to long term, except direct mortality events.
Overall significance: EDI agreed with BMC’s conclusion that residual effects are not significant — they are adverse but low in magnitude, and the FCH population is not expected to be affected at the regional scale given effective mitigation.

section: 3.4 Key limiting factors and mitigation context
text:
3.4 Key limiting factors and mitigation context
What actually limits the FCH?
EDI noted that habitat is not the primary limiting factor for the FCH. The response of the herd to the 1983–1989 wolf control program — growing from ~2,000 to ~5,950 animals — clearly demonstrates that predation and hunting mortality are the dominant drivers of population dynamics. The Project, by contrast, directly affects less than 1% of key seasonal habitat.
Why indirect effects are discounted at 50%
Following Dyer et al. (2001), who studied woodland caribou avoidance of industrial roads in Alberta: caribou significantly avoided habitat within 0–250 m of roads, but avoidance was not statistically significant beyond 250 m. This means that indirect habitat effects do not constitute a complete functional loss — hence the 50% weighting applied to indirect habitat loss in the EA.
Mitigation measures proposed by BMC (and endorsed by EDI)







Measure
Target effect




Traffic management plan
Reduce vehicle collision risk


Restricting public access from Robert Campbell Highway
Prevent induced hunting


Using existing disturbed areas (Tote Road, exploration footprint)
Limit new habitat loss


Avoiding core alpine rut/post-calving habitat where possible
Reduce disturbance to key life stages


Wildlife monitoring program with adaptive management triggers
Allow timely response to unexpected effects



EDI’s overall conclusion (2019)

“In EDI’s opinion, based on the information presented in the Project Proposal and the AAR1 and AAR2 responses, the predicted residual effects of the Project, relative to baseline conditions, are not likely to affect the viability of the FCH within their home range in Yukon.”
EDI also noted: “If mortality factors such as wolf predation and hunting are managed, caribou may be able to co-exist with well managed developments.”

Note that this assessment was conducted in 2019 using the 2017 census (2,712 animals) as baseline. The 2022 census (3,359 animals) indicates the herd has since grown, which would further support a conclusion of low project-level significance relative to herd viability.

title: 4  Population Estimates
text:
7.1 How the surveys work
All seven population estimates of the Finlayson caribou herd (1986, 1990, 1996, 1999, 2007, 2017, 2022) have used the same core approach: a stratified random block (SRB) survey originally developed for moose by Farnell & Gauthier (1988) and adapted for woodland caribou in the Yukon.


7.1.1 Step 1 — Stratification (fixed-wing)
Prior to the intensive count, experienced observers fly a small fixed-wing aircraft (typically a Cessna 206) through all ~214 survey blocks covering the ~6,780 km² winter range. Each block is classified into one of three strata based on caribou presence and fresh sign (tracks, feeding craters):

Primary (high use) — ≥ 12 caribou observed or abundant fresh sign
Secondary (low use) — < 12 caribou, or limited fresh sign
Out — no caribou and no recent sign

Snow conditions are critical here. In 2022, recent snowfall before the survey made fresh tracks easy to distinguish from old ones — conditions were described as ideal. In 2017, a gap of several weeks without snowfall made track interpretation difficult; the initial stratification had to be redone post-hoc using a density threshold of 1 caribou/km².



7.1.2 Step 2 — Census (helicopter)
Two helicopters (typically Bell Jet Rangers with three observers each) fly all primary blocks and a random selection of secondary blocks, running parallel transects approximately 400 m apart across each block at an intensity of roughly 2 minutes per km². Two helicopters operate simultaneously to minimise the chance of animals moving between blocks during the survey. Each caribou group is:

Counted
Classified into cows, calves, young bulls, and mature bulls
Located by GPS




7.1.3 Step 3 — Extrapolation for unsurveyed secondaries
Because only a subset of secondary blocks is flown, the average caribou density observed in surveyed secondaries is applied to all secondary blocks (surveyed and unsurveyed) to estimate total abundance in that stratum. This is the main source of statistical uncertainty — if sampled secondaries happen to have atypically high or low densities, the extrapolation will be biased. The 2022 report notes this may have slightly inflated the final estimate, since bull-dominated groups (more broadly distributed) were likely over-represented in randomly selected secondary blocks.



7.1.4 Step 4 — Sightability correction factor (SCF)
Aerial surveys inevitably miss some animals. A sightability correction factor is applied to scale up the raw counts. In 1986, 1990, 1996, and 1999, dedicated sightability trials were run (n = 43 total): an area just counted was immediately re-flown at higher intensity to find missed animals. A logistic regression model fitted to all 43 trials estimated a sightability rate of 77.6% (SE = 0.037), equivalent to a correction multiplier of 1.289 (SE = 0.061). This same factor — derived from the historic trials — was applied in both 2017 and 2022, since resources were not available for new trials.

title: 4  Population Estimates
section: 7.3 Why winter surveys? And why not mark-resight?
text:
7.3 Why winter surveys? And why not mark-resight?
Why survey in late winter?
FCH census surveys are conducted in late February to mid-March, when animals are grouped on their lowland winter range. This has practical advantages: animals are concentrated in a fraction of the total range (~1,400–1,800 km² out of ~6,780 km²), making intensive helicopter coverage feasible; fresh snow improves track detection during stratification; and sightability is generally better in open, low-canopy lichen woodland than in alpine terrain.
Alternative timing is possible but harder. Calving and post-calving surveys face three key challenges noted by Environment Yukon (Morgan, pers. comm. 2025): cows are widely dispersed across the range during calving; individual cows are solitary and difficult to locate; and sightability in rugged alpine terrain is lower. These factors would substantially reduce survey efficiency and increase cost.
Why not use mark-resight?
Since the mid-2000s, Yukon’s caribou program has used a mark-resight approach for all other Northern Mountain herds: GPS collars are deployed on adult females, who serve as known “marks.” During the fall rut — when animals concentrate at high-elevation sub-alpine habitats — observers record the ratio of marked to unmarked animals, producing a statistically more precise population estimate and yielding multiple years of detailed annual distribution and movement data (Morgan, pers. comm. 2025; see also Coal River Caribou Herd 2022 Population Estimate).
The Finlayson herd cannot use this method for two reasons:

Cultural: The Kaska First Nations, in whose traditional territory the herd lives, have not supported the collaring of animals since the 1990s. Between 1982 and 1987, 52 VHF collars were deployed with at least 20 relocations per collar, providing useful survival and distribution data; however, collaring was not continued as it did not receive support from community partners (Russell et al. 2022). The Government of Yukon has respected this position since.
Consistency: Maintaining the SRB method preserves direct comparability with all seven previous censuses back to 1986, making the long-term trend reliable even if the absolute numbers carry some systematic bias.

The 2022 report recommends exploring novel survey methods that do not require collared animals — options might include aerial photogrammetry or distance sampling — to improve precision while respecting community values.

title: 4  Population Estimates
text:
8.3 Harvest history and regulations
The Finlayson herd is an important subsistence resource for the Ross River Dena Council and Liard First Nation (Kaska). Harvest management has evolved as the herd declined:

Pre-1998: Open licensed hunting; outfitters active. Highest licensed harvest occurred in the early 1990s, coinciding with the post-wolf-control population peak.
1996–2004: A winter game guardian program along the Robert Campbell Highway documented subsistence harvest — including cow harvest, which has a disproportionate population impact (1 cow ≈ 3 bulls in harvest equivalence terms).
1998: PHA introduced — 30 permits for resident hunters; outfitters placed on quota. The sustainable harvest level was set at 3% of the ~4,000-animal 1996 estimate (120 animals), split 75% First Nations / 25% licensed.
2018–2019: All licensed and non-resident harvest closed following continued decline to 2,712 animals in 2017.
Current: Subsistence harvest by First Nations continues. Historical estimates suggest subsistence alone may equal or exceed the 1% bull-only threshold (≈27 animals) considered sustainable for a declining herd.


Winter range characteristics
The core winter range lies north of the Pelly Mountains east of Ross River — a lowland forested area with abundant ground lichens under open black spruce, white spruce, and lodgepole pine. The Pelly Mountains create a snow-shadow effect, producing low snow cover ideal for lichen access. The spring/summer/fall range in the Pelly Mountains overlaps an active mineral exploration belt, creating ongoing concerns about cumulative industrial effects on the herd.

title: 5  Seasonal Ranges
text:
5.1 Seasonal Habitat Ranges
The Finlayson Caribou Herd (FCH), a sub-type of woodland caribou designated as a population of Special Concern, requires large, contiguous landscapes to support its survival as it migrates between seasonally distinct but overlapping ranges. The Kudz Ze Kayah Project is uniquely situated at the intersection of these critical ranges, including late winter, calving, post-calving, rut, and early winter habitats.

title: 5  Seasonal Ranges
text:
Winter Range: During late winter, the herd primarily occupies lowland areas around the Robert Campbell Highway and north toward Ross River. In recent years, there has been a shift in use toward the area surrounding Finlayson Lake, which overlaps the northern portion of the Project area. This range is vital because it supports a high density of animals during a period when snow depth and cold temperatures make foraging energetically demanding.
Calving Range: In late May and early June, pregnant cows disperse into high mountainous terrain to increase calf survival by avoiding predators. Suitable and occupied calving habitat exists at higher elevations throughout the Project area.
Post-Calving Range: Following calving, caribou utilize subalpine and alpine areas, often seeking snow patches to avoid insects. The Project area contains core post-calving habitat where cows and calves congregate to access high-quality forage necessary for calf development.
Rutting Range: The rut occurs in October, primarily on alpine ridges and plateaus. A large proportion of the total FCH population congregates in areas immediately adjacent to the mine site during this time, utilizing traditional sites with high site fidelity.




Figure 5-1 – Finlayson caribou herd seasonal distribution and habitat ranges

title: 5  Seasonal Ranges
text:
5.2 Movement Corridors and Connectivity
The Project is located in an area recognized by Kaska knowledge holders as a “caribou crossing” and an essential portal to calving grounds in the mountains to the south. A well-documented migration corridor extends approximately 4 km above and below the confluence of Geona and Finlayson Creeks. Maintaining landscape connectivity is crucial for the herd to move effectively between these seasonal ranges to fulfill their life cycle requirements.

title: 5  Seasonal Ranges
text:
5.3 Project Impacts on Distribution
Modeling conducted by the Proponent indicates that the project will result in the direct removal of 5% of high-quality rutting habitat and 4% of high-quality post-calving habitat within the core of the herd’s range. While these percentages were quantified, the Executive Committee highlighted that calving habitat and movement corridors were not modeled, which they characterized as a “significant knowledge gap”. The concentration of caribou in the region during the rut makes a significant proportion of the population vulnerable to sensory disturbances from project activities, which may lead to displacement and permanent avoidance of these traditional ranges.

title: 6  Habitat requirements
text:
6.1 Seasonal range overview
The Finlayson caribou herd (FCH) is a Northern Mountain (NM) woodland caribou population (Rangifer tarandus caribou) that undertakes pronounced seasonal migrations between low-elevation winter range and high-elevation alpine/subalpine summer range. Northern Mountain caribou migrate seasonally, moving from the open boreal forest in winter up into the subalpine and alpine in summer — though some herds also spend much of the winter on windswept alpine slopes. The table below summarises the FCH’s known seasonal habitat associations, drawn from the population survey reports and the broader Northern Mountain caribou literature.
Season
Elevation / terrain
Key habitat features
Primary forage




Winter (Dec – Mar)
Low-elevation lowland forest; sheltered from prevailing SW weather by Pelly Mountains
Open black spruce, white spruce, lodgepole pine forest with abundant ground lichens; low snow due to mountain rain shadow
Terrestrial lichens (Cladonia/Cladina spp.) excavated by cratering through snow


Spring (Apr – May)
Transitional; animals move from lowland winter range upward; females typically lead
South-facing slopes and riparian areas that snow-free early; access to fresh green vegetation
Early green-up: forbs, sedges, new shrub growth; supplemented by lichens


Calving / post-calving (May – Jun)
High elevation subalpine/alpine; females disperse widely and are largely solitary
Isolated subalpine/parkland habitat; low moose density reduces wolf presence (predator avoidance)
Forbs, sedges, graminoids; diverse high-quality forage to support lactation


Summer (Jul – Sep)
Upper subalpine and alpine plateaus south of Finlayson Lake; ~1/3 of herd uses alpine north of Robert Campbell Hwy
Open alpine tundra, sedge meadows, insect-relief habitat (ridges, icefalls, snowfields)
Forbs, graminoids, dwarf shrubs, fungi, sedges; diverse diet

title: 6  Habitat requirements
text:
6.2 Winter habitat — the critical season
Lichen as the keystone winter resource
Northern Mountain caribou are the only animals that forage substantially on lichen in the winter. Terrestrial lichens are the winter forage species of most importance to northern caribou. Caribou excavate these through the snowpack using their broad hooves in a behaviour called cratering — consuming roughly 3 kg of lichen per day. Snow depth significantly affects access to this critical food: once snow exceeds approximately 50 centimetres, even high-lichen areas become inaccessible.
The FCH’s core winter range east of Ross River benefits from a pronounced snow-shadow effect created by the Pelly Mountains intercepting moisture-laden weather systems from the southwest, keeping snow shallow and making lichen accessible throughout the winter. This is precisely why snow-depth anomalies matter: in 2007, deeper-than-normal snow near Caribou Lakes pushed the majority of the herd east toward the shallower snowpack around Finlayson Lake — an unusual distribution not seen in any previous survey.
Lichen characteristics and recovery time
Winter lichen availability is critical to evaluating caribou habitat. Highest densities are associated with mature forests, as lichen is very slow growing. Growth rates of reindeer lichen groups (Cladonia spp.) are approximately 5 mm per year, and the long recovery time for lichen forage has been suggested as a limiting factor for caribou populations. This slow recovery makes lichen mats highly vulnerable to disturbance — whether from fire, industrial footprint, or overgrazing — and explains why old-growth and mature forest stands are disproportionately important.
Northern mountain caribou rely on old growth forests because they have abundant amounts of terrestrial and arboreal lichen, and shallow snow depth due to interception by the canopy. Windswept areas also have shallow snow due to wind, which allows access to terrestrial lichen. Winter habitat is often in areas where a rain or snow shadow is present, which results in reduced precipitation.
Flexibility between lichen types
In winter, caribou forage on terrestrial lichens in both lowland lodgepole pine flats and on windswept alpine slopes, and on arboreal lichens in upper elevation Engelmann spruce and subalpine fir forests. In a year of record heavy snowfall, all collared caribou wintered on windswept alpine slopes, while during the below-average snowfall year, many remained in forested habitats. In late winter, when increased snow depths make cratering for terrestrial lichens difficult, caribou feed increasingly on arboreal lichens.

title: 6  Habitat requirements
section: 6.3 Predator avoidance as a habitat driver
text:
6.3 Predator avoidance as a habitat driver
For Northern Mountain caribou, habitat selection is not solely about forage — predator avoidance is an equally powerful force shaping where and when caribou use the landscape. This is especially important for understanding the FCH, whose primary limiting factor has been wolf predation rather than food availability.
Spatial separation from moose and wolves
The core mechanism is apparent competition: wolves primarily hunt moose, but will take caribou opportunistically. Where moose are abundant, wolf numbers are sustained at levels that inflict significant mortality on caribou. Caribou avoid predation primarily by spatially segregating from other ungulate species that are the primary prey of their shared predators. Selection of fen/bog complexes by caribou and selection of well-drained habitats by moose and wolves results in spatial separation, which in turn reduces wolf predation pressure on caribou — but does not provide a total refuge from wolves.
For mountain herds like the FCH, the equivalent mechanism is elevational separation: caribou use high alpine and subalpine habitat during calving and summer — terrain that wolves travel through less efficiently and where moose are largely absent. During calving, females are dispersed from moose and other wolf prey by selecting high elevation subalpine and parkland habitats.
Response to industrial linear features
All large mammal predator and prey species move faster on linear features (roads, cutlines). Wolves and bears are attracted towards linear features, whereas prey species avoid them. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that linear features facilitate predator movement and increase hunting efficiency, while prey perceive such features as risky.
This has direct relevance to the KZK mine Access Road: while caribou avoidance beyond 250 m is not statistically significant (Dyer et al. 2001), the road may still elevate effective predation risk by enabling faster wolf travel through the FCH’s rut and early winter range.
Disturbance avoidance and range fidelity
In summer, caribou avoided mines by 2 km and cabins and camps by 1.5 km, while in winter, when human activity was low, avoidance of these features was minor. This seasonal asymmetry is relevant to the FCH: the KZK mine would be most active during seasons when caribou are present for rutting and post-calving — the periods of highest avoidance response.
General caribou-habitat relationships — selection of conifer-dominated forests and treed lowlands, and avoidance of disturbed, settled and open areas and roads — are consistent with current management guidance. Fidelity is strongest for calving sites and home ranges used during the calving and post-calving seasons.

Why habitat is not the current limiting factor for the FCH
The EDI review (2019) and the population reports both emphasise that, unlike many boreal caribou populations in southern Canada where habitat loss from logging is the primary driver of decline, the FCH’s trajectory has been governed principally by mortality — specifically wolf predation and harvest. The Pelly Mountains winter range remains largely intact old-growth lichen forest with low industrial footprint, and the snow-shadow microclimate has not substantially changed. This distinction is important for management: actions targeting predation and harvest regulation (as implemented 2018–2019) are expected to be more effective than habitat protection alone at stabilising this particular herd.

title: 7  Habitat suitability
text:
8 Introduction
The Kudz Ze Kayah (KZK) Project is a proposed base-metal mine in the Yukon Plateau-North Ecoregion of the Canadian Boreal Cordillera Ecozone, approximately 260 km northwest of Watson Lake and 115 km southeast of Ross River, Yukon. The Project lies within the traditional home range of the Finlayson caribou herd (FCH), a population of Northern Mountain caribou (Rangifer tarandus caribou) assessed by the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC) as a Species of Special Concern, and listed as such under the federal Species at Risk Act (SARA) in 2005. The FCH is of significant ecological, economic, and cultural importance to the Kaska First Nation, resident and guided hunters, and the general public.
The federal Management Plan for the Northern Mountain Population of Woodland Caribou directs responsible agencies to (i) identify and assess the quality, quantity, and distribution of important caribou habitats, and (ii) manage and conserve those habitats. To meet these objectives at the KZK Project site, Alexco Environmental Group Inc. (AEG) developed a series of habitat suitability index (HSI) models for the FCH, built from over three decades of Yukon Government survey data supplemented by project-specific surveys carried out by AEG between 2015 and 2017.
Three life-requisite seasons were modelled:
The purpose of each HSI was to predict the spatial distribution of suitable caribou habitat within the Local Study Area (LSA) — a 3 km buffer around proposed mine infrastructure and a 1.5 km buffer around the Tote/Access Road — and across the FCH’s traditional home range (~23,000 km²), in order to support the design of avoidance and mitigation measures and to assess potential residual effects of the Project on caribou habitat.
This workbook consolidates the background, methods, and results reported across these documents and reproduces the key summary statistics, membership functions, and results tables using R.

title: 7  Habitat suitability
text:
8.1 Study Area
The Project sits in the Geona Creek valley in the northeastern foothills of the Pelly Mountains, straddling the subalpine and lower alpine zones. Treeline occurs at approximately 1,550 m above sea level (masl); above 1,700 masl the landscape transitions to alpine tundra dominated by dwarf shrub, graminoid, and lichen cover. The Tote Road/Access Road corridor parallels the lower reaches of Finlayson Creek through open white and black spruce forest.
The FCH is an elevational, migratory ecotype. In spring, roughly two-thirds of the herd move from wintering grounds near the Pelly River to calve in the highlands of the southeastern Pelly Mountains; the remainder travel to mountains northeast of Finlayson Lake. Through summer, caribou disperse onto alpine plateaus and ridges to avoid predators and to seek relief from insects and heat, aggregating again in open alpine/subalpine habitat for the fall rut (peaking mid-October). In late fall the herd migrates northwest back toward the Pelly lowlands, becoming increasingly reliant on terrestrial lichen (roughly 70% of the winter diet) as green forage senesces. In late winter, the FCH concentrates in the low-elevation forest and shrublands around the Pelly River and Finlayson Lake, an area that sits in an orographic rain/snow-shadow north of the Pelly Mountains and typically receives less than 30 cm of precipitation annually — far below snow depths (50–90 cm) known to impede caribou mobility.

title: 7  Habitat suitability
text:
8.2 Habitat Selection
Caribou habitat requirements vary strongly by season, which is the ecological basis for building season-specific HSI models rather than a single year-round model:

Spring/calving (Apr–Jun): migration to calving grounds; solitary, high-visibility alpine sites or concealing subalpine cover, away from alternate prey (e.g., moose) that support predator populations.
Summer/post-calving (Jun–Sep): dispersal into small groups on upper subalpine/alpine ridges, plateaus and upper-elevation streams; forage on forbs, deciduous leaves, lichens, fungi, grasses, and sedges; use of windy ridges and snow patches for insect and heat relief.
Fall/rut (peaks mid-October): aggregation in open alpine and subalpine habitat; 2015–2016 early winter surveys found FCH remaining on rutting grounds in the Project area until mid-December.
Migration (late fall/spring): transit through boreal forest, subalpine, shrubland, and alpine tundra; diet shifts toward terrestrial lichen as herbaceous forage dies off.
Late winter: concentration in low-elevation, low-snowpack forest/shrubland in the Pelly River–Finlayson Lake snow-shadow, where shallow snow allows cratering to access terrestrial lichen.

Winter habitat suitability was not modelled in the original 2016 report because the traditional core winter range lies ~100 km northwest of the Project site, outside the Project’s zone of influence (ZOI); the model was added later at YESAB’s request because the herd’s late-winter range overlaps the Access Road corridor.

title: 7  Habitat suitability
text:
9.2 Variables and Fuzzy Membership Functions
Four environmental variables were evaluated for the rut and post-calving models — elevation, slope, aspect, and vegetation cover — chosen because they are ecologically meaningful, well supported in the literature, and available continuously across the entire FCH home range. The late-winter model substituted winter precipitation for aspect (aspect showed no distributional signal in low-relief winter range and was dropped).
Elevation, slope, and precipitation were treated as continuous variables and rescaled to a 0–1 suitability index using a linear fuzzy membership function, with breakpoints set from the frequency distribution of calibration-data locations along each variable. Aspect and vegetation cover are discrete/categorical variables, ranked 0–1 directly from observation frequency in each class and refined with expert opinion.

9.2.1 Elevation





Fuzzy membership functions for elevation suitability, by season




Post-calving suitability peaks at higher elevation (1,600–1,900 masl) than rut (1,500–1,800 masl), consistent with caribou seeking high ridges/plateaus for predator, heat, and insect avoidance during summer. Late-winter suitability is highest at low elevation (≤1,000 masl) and declines to zero by 1,500 masl, reflecting the herd’s descent into the Pelly River/Finlayson Lake lowlands.


9.2.2 Slope





Fuzzy membership functions for slope suitability, by season




Rut habitat is most suitable on gentle terrain (≤25°), falling to zero by 60°. Post-calving habitat tolerates a wider plateau of moderate slope (10°–50°), consistent with use of ridges and upper plateaus. Late-winter habitat is essentially flat-terrain habitat, with suitability collapsing above ~12.5°, reflecting use of the lowland forest/shrub mosaic rather than mountain terrain.

title: 7  Habitat suitability
text:
9.3 Model Development
For each season, the reclassified variable layers (each rescaled 0–1) were resampled to a common 25 m grid, multiplied by an importance weight, and summed to produce a single continuous suitability surface (0–1). Aspect and vegetation (categorical, less discriminating) generally received lower weights than elevation and slope; for the late-winter model, all four variables were weighted evenly:
\[\text{Late winter HSI} = 0.25 \times \text{Elevation} + 0.25 \times \text{Slope} + 0.25 \times \text{Vegetation} + 0.25 \times \text{Precipitation}\]
Focal statistics (a 100 m / 4-cell radius smoothing window) were then applied to remove isolated single-cell artifacts and produce a spatially continuous surface, and the result was reclassified into six ordinal habitat classes (Nil, Very Low, Low, Moderate, Moderately High, High) following the British Columbia Wildlife Habitat Rating Standards (RIC 1999).

title: 7  Habitat suitability
text:
9.4 Model Evaluation
Models were evaluated using the non-parametric Kendall tau test, chosen over Spearman’s rank correlation because it is less sensitive to error and performs better with smaller sample sizes. The test assessed whether the six ordinal HSI classes were correlated with the density of independent aerial survey observations (i.e., data withheld from model calibration). A model was accepted as statistically significant at α = 0.05, and where multiple candidate weighting/breakpoint schemes were tested, the version with the highest tau coefficient (strongest correlation) was retained as final. All statistics were computed in R (R Core Team 2014).

title: 8  Seasonal movements
text:
8.1 Annual migration cycle
The FCH undertakes a pronounced annual elevational migration between its low-elevation winter range and high-elevation summer range — a pattern typical of Northern Mountain woodland caribou but distinct from more sedentary boreal populations. The seasonal cycle is driven by three interacting forces: forage availability, predator avoidance, and insect relief. The ability to move freely between seasonal ranges is considered vitally important for Northern Mountain caribou populations (Environment Canada 2012).
The diagram below summarises the approximate timing and direction of seasonal movements for the FCH based on survey report observations, radio-collar data from the 1982–1987 collaring program, and the broader Northern Mountain caribou literature.

title: 8  Seasonal movements
text:
8.2 Phase-by-phase movement description
Late winter (December – March)
The majority of the FCH winters on the lowland lichen-rich forests east of Ross River, north of the Pelly Mountains. Animals are most concentrated during this period — a key reason why late-winter surveys are logistically feasible. The core winter range lies on both sides of the Robert Campbell Highway. Approximately one-third of the herd uses a separate group of alpine blocks north of the Highway, ranging close to the NWT border. This spatial split appears consistent across survey years.
The precise location of wintering animals within the range shifts between years depending on snow depth. In most years, the bulk of the herd winters near Caribou Lakes; however, in 2007 deeper-than-normal snow there pushed animals east toward Finlayson Lake — an unusual distribution not documented in any prior survey (Adamczewski et al. 2010). More recently (2022), the herd was again concentrated south of the Highway in the Caribou Lakes area, more consistent with the historical 1986–1999 pattern.

Spring migration (April – May)
As snow begins to melt, caribou move from lowland winter range upward toward spring and summer range. In spring, caribou move from high elevation winter ranges to lower elevation habitat, primarily lodgepole pine and lodgepole pine–white spruce dominated stands. In early spring, caribou seek new green vegetation in bogs, riparian areas, and open meadows. Use of habitats such as south-facing deciduous hillsides and meadows that become snow-free earlier than heavily timbered areas is common. Pregnant females typically lead the spring migration, ascending to summer ranges before males.

Calving (late May – June)
Calving occurs in late May to early June on high-elevation subalpine and alpine/parkland habitats, primarily on alpine plateaus south of Finlayson Lake. During calving, females are widely dispersed and largely solitary — making this the most difficult season for aerial survey work. The isolation of calving females from other ungulates (and thus from wolves, whose numbers are sustained by moose) is considered an active anti-predator strategy. Calving caribou were not found within the Kudz Ze Kayah project footprint during wildlife baseline surveys (BMC 2017).

Post-calving summer (July – September)
After calving, cows with calves aggregate into larger groups, often seeking wind-exposed ridges, icefalls, and snowfields to escape harassment by insects (mosquitoes, black flies, bot flies, warble flies). Summer range consists primarily of upper-elevation spruce/fir forest and subalpine/alpine areas. Summer diet is more diverse than in winter, consisting of forbs, deciduous leaves, lichens, fungi, grasses, and sedges. The FCH’s core summer and fall range is on alpine plateaus south of Finlayson Lake, overlapping the Pelly Mountains mineral exploration belt.

Rut / fall (October – November)
The annual rut occurs in October–November on alpine and subalpine range. During this period bulls seek out concentrated cow groups, and animals aggregate at higher elevations — the timing exploited by the mark-resight method used for all other Yukon Northern Mountain herds. The FCH’s rut range overlaps significantly with the proposed Kudz Ze Kayah mine area, making this the period of greatest potential Project–caribou interaction (BMC 2017; Johannesen & Setterington 2019).

Early winter descent (November – December)
As winter weather sets in and snow deepens at higher elevations, caribou descend back to their lowland winter range to access terrestrial lichens. The timing and route of this descent may vary by individual, with some animals lingering at mid-elevations before moving fully to the winter range.

title: 8  Seasonal movements
text:
8.3 Sex-specific spatial segregation in winter
A consistent and ecologically important pattern documented across all FCH surveys is the spatial segregation of bulls from cows and calves during winter. This was first documented in early March surveys and is now well-established:

Bull-dominated groups (> 50% bulls) tend to be smaller (averaging 3–22 individuals in 2022), distributed more broadly, often north of the Robert Campbell Highway, and in the more western portion of the study area.
Cow-dominated groups (< 50% bulls) tend to be larger (averaging 13 individuals in 2022), concentrated south of the Highway, with distribution extending further east.

In 2007, of the 228 mature bulls counted, 198 (86.8%) were in all-bull groups, mostly north and west of the Pelly River (Adamczewski et al. 2010). This pattern has been consistently observed across the 1986, 1990, 1996, 1999, 2007, 2017, and 2022 surveys.
Why does segregation occur?
Sex-biased winter distribution in caribou is well-documented and is believed to result from antlered cows (who retain their antlers through winter, unlike bulls who shed theirs in November) gathering and defending limited, high-quality foraging areas to ensure adequate nutrition during pregnancy. This gives pregnant cows priority access to the richest lichen patches, with bulls displaced to secondary areas. The pattern has important survey implications: randomly selected secondary blocks have a higher probability of containing bull-only groups, which may inflate population estimates when those densities are extrapolated to unsurveyed blocks (Russell & Russell 2022).

title: 8  Seasonal movements
text:
8.4 Range fidelity and variability
Site fidelity across years
FCH animals display moderate range fidelity — returning to the same general seasonal ranges across years, but with considerable within-season flexibility depending on snow conditions, lichen availability, and disturbance. Fidelity is strongest for calving sites and weakest for winter home ranges (Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources 2023), a pattern consistent with the FCH’s documented inter-annual variation in winter distribution.
The 2007 distributional anomaly
The 2007 census documented a striking departure from the established pattern: nearly two-thirds of the herd (1,645 of 2,522 uncorrected animals) was found near Finlayson Lake, whereas in all previous surveys (1986, 1990, 1996, 1999) the majority wintered near Caribou Lakes. Post-survey snow-depth measurements along the Robert Campbell Highway confirmed that snow was deeper than normal near Caribou Lakes in 2007, while conditions near Finlayson Lake were unusually shallow — consistent with animals tracking accessible lichen rather than exhibiting true fidelity to a specific site (Adamczewski et al. 2010).
The 2022 return to historical distribution
By 2022 the distribution had reverted toward the historical pattern, with most animals concentrated south of the Highway in the Caribou Lakes area and few near Finlayson Lake. This shift was noted as analogous to observations from the 1986–1999 surveys. It may reflect a return to normal snow conditions, or could indicate that animals making less predictable use of winter locations have higher survival by avoiding wolf ambush — consistent with evidence that reduced range fidelity in winter can be an adaptive predator-avoidance strategy (Lafontaine et al. 2017).
Movement rates and distances
Formal movement data are limited for this herd given the absence of collars since the 1990s. The 52 VHF collars deployed from 1982 to 1987 (with ≥ 20 relocations per collar) provided foundational data on adult female survival rates and seasonal distribution patterns (Farnell et al. 2008), but detailed step-length or daily movement data comparable to GPS-collar studies on other herds are not available. This represents a key knowledge gap that novel non-invasive survey technologies could help address.
